Dereplication feasibility – all 25 participants

2026-09-06

Context

Same-participant longitudinal metagenomics (25 participants: 19 with both a pooled co-assembly and multiple single-sample assemblies, 6 with single-sample assemblies only) means a lot of the sequence assembled and annotated across samples is likely near-identical repeat, not independent new information. This report tests that directly with mmseqs2 clustering at two levels – contigs (Tier 1, feeds geNomad/MAP’s contig-level tools) and ORFs/genes (Tier 2, feeds funcscan’s AMR/AMP/CAZyme tools) – across all 25 participants, then cross-checks the core assumption (that clustered = safe to annotate once and propagate) against already-computed real production annotation (RGI, geNomad), with no new annotation compute. See dereplication_brainstorm.md for the original design and dereplication_pilot_results.md for the 2-participant pilot this scales up.

Gene-level (Tier 2) redundancy sits at 90%+ for essentially every participant; contig-level (Tier 1) redundancy is lower and more variable (roughly 40-45%), consistent with contigs being longer, structurally-specific sequences while genes are shorter, more conserved units.

2. Gene cluster: co-assembly vs. single-sample

3. Contig cluster: co-assembly vs. single-sample

4. Co-assembly-unique contribution

Contigs/genes in a cluster with no single-sample member at all – only recoverable by pooling reads across timepoints, not by any individual single-sample assembly.

Caveat: a co-assembly-only cluster could reflect genuinely novel sequence only assemblable with pooled coverage (the real win) – or a chimeric misassembly artifact from stitching together similar-but-distinct strain variants across timepoints (a known risk of pooled co-assembly). This number doesn’t distinguish the two.

Concretely, for AMR genes specifically: 607 real resistance gene hits across all 19 co-assembly participants were found only via the co-assembly – no single-sample assembly recovered them independently.

5. AMR gene redundancy

Across all 296 assemblies, RGI reported 51,654 raw AMR gene hits, collapsing to 12,227 truly distinct AMR genes once dereplicated (76.3% redundant) – notably lower than the general gene-level redundancy (90%+), meaning AMR genes show more real diversity across timepoints/samples than a typical core gene.

6. Parameter sensitivity sweep

Participant Tier Setting Redundant (count %) Redundant (bp %)
p110 contigs cov-mode 2 (original) 43.9 71.4
p110 contigs cov-mode 0 20.8 34.4
p110 orfs min-seq-id 0.95 (original) 93.2 96.0
p110 orfs min-seq-id 0.99 90.6 94.0
p97 contigs cov-mode 2 (original) 42.0 73.3
p97 contigs cov-mode 0 25.1 47.8
p97 orfs min-seq-id 0.95 (original) 96.5 98.0
p97 orfs min-seq-id 0.99 94.4 96.4

Tier 2 (genes) is robust to identity threshold (95%->99% barely moves the number) – the gene-level redundancy signal is real, not a loose-threshold artifact. Tier 1 (contigs) is highly sensitive to --cov-mode: switching from containment-aware (query-coverage) to bidirectional coverage roughly halves the redundancy fraction – expected, since bidirectional coverage misses the “same region assembled to different lengths at different depths” scenario this analysis targets. The original settings (cov-mode 2, min-seq-id 0.95) were kept.

7. Propagation validation: does clustering predict identical annotation?

For clusters where >=2 members independently received a real hit from RGI (genes) or geNomad (contigs), do they agree?

Tool Testable clusters Consistent Inconsistent % consistent
RGI 9411 9075 336 96.4
geNomad 29071 28503 568 98.0

Both tools show strong (96-98%) agreement. The disagreements are not random – inspection of individual cases showed:

  • RGI disagreements concentrate almost entirely on vanY/vanT/vanXY genes assigned to different van-operon subtypes (vanA vs vanB vs vanG vs vanM) – a known CARD/RGI database ambiguity for this highly homologous gene family, not a dereplication failure.
  • geNomad disagreements are plasmid-vs-virus classification flips, consistent with genuine prophage-plasmid hybrid mobile elements the classifier finds genuinely borderline.

8. Gene cluster longitudinal similarity within participant

For every pair of a participant’s own single-sample timepoints: what fraction of gene clusters do they share (Jaccard), vs. real calendar days between them?

Similarity is highest (~0.6-0.8) for timepoints ~1-2 weeks apart and drops substantially (~0.2-0.3) for timepoints roughly a year apart – real strain turnover, not noise. This matters directly for the propagation design: an “annotate once” representative may not stay valid indefinitely over a long study and could need periodic refresh.

9. Within- vs. between-participant sharing (second-level clustering)

Each participant’s own already-deduplicated representatives, clustered again across all 25 participants – a cluster with members from >1 participant means that sequence is shared across different people, not just across one person’s timepoints.

Tier Within-participant only Between-participant Total % between
contigs 2424701 1056731 3481432 30.4
orfs 1446992 1147512 2594504 44.2

Genes are shared across participants far more than contigs (44% vs. 30% of clusters span >=2 people) – genes are smaller, more conserved units that recombine/transfer more readily, while contigs carry more participant/strain-specific structural context. This means the full cohort dereplication opportunity is larger than the within-participant numbers above suggest – including real, concrete cases of the same AMR gene (e.g. adeF) recurring in different, unrelated participants.

10. Contig cluster x plasmid classification x AMR genes

Category N clusters N AMR-carrying % AMR-carrying
plasmid 57782 1187 2.05
virus 53127 282 0.53
other 5366483 27576 0.51

Plasmid-classified contig clusters carry an AMR gene at roughly 4x the background rate; virus-classified clusters show no enrichment over background – matches expected mobile-genetic-element biology (plasmids as a classic AMR reservoir/vector, unlike phages), recovered here from real, cluster-deduplicated data rather than assumed.

Conclusions

  1. Real, large, robust redundancy at both tiers, across all 25 participants – not just the original 2-participant pilot. Gene-level redundancy (90%+) is essentially uniform; contig-level redundancy (~40-45%) is more variable but still substantial.
  2. The core propagation assumption holds (96-98% consistent for both a gene-level and a contig-level tool), with disagreements traceable to known, specific classifier ambiguities rather than random noise – a real annotate-representative-and-propagate pipeline is justified.
  3. Co-assembly earns its computational cost: recovers real AMR genes (607 instances) and substantial contig/gene content that no single-sample assembly would have, though a fraction of that may be pooling artifact rather than genuine novel sequence.
  4. Cross-participant sharing is real and non-trivial, especially for genes (44%) – a full cohort-wide dereplication (not just within-participant) would capture meaningfully more redundancy than reported here.
  5. Time matters: gene-sharing between timepoints decays with real calendar time – an eventual production pipeline should account for this rather than treat “annotate once” as valid indefinitely.

Not yet done: per-tool propagation-safety audit beyond RGI/geNomad (the brainstorm’s original open question), and no representative-annotation + propagation pipeline has been built yet – this report is the evidence base for deciding whether to build one.
